weeks.title: Light, Exposure and Tonal Storytelling
weeks.essential: How can light, exposure and tonal structure change what an image communicates without changing the subject itself?

vocab.Exposure: The amount of light recorded or represented in an image.
vocab.Dynamic range: The span from the darkest usable tone to the lightest usable tone.
vocab.Direction of light: The angle from which light reaches a subject, shaping highlights, shadows and volume.
vocab.Ethical editing: Disclosed adjustments that improve readability without misrepresenting evidence or context.

weeks.worked: Place one simple object near a window or lamp. Make three studies—front-lit, side-lit and back-lit—while keeping subject and viewpoint stable. Compare value pattern, edge clarity and mood. Revise one tonal relationship and disclose exactly what changed.
stages: Observe one object under at least three light directions and identify highlight, halftone, core shadow, cast shadow and reflected light where visible.
Research two attributed photographs or paintings that use lighting deliberately; record creator, title, date when known, source and lighting purpose.
Create three controlled light studies plus one exposure or tonal comparison. A camera is optional; graphite, charcoal or value blocks fully count.
Ask a reviewer which tonal relationship is clearest. Revise one study to improve value separation while preserving the original.
Explain what lighting changed, what it did not prove, what editing occurred and one lighting choice you will carry forward.
weeks.assignment: Submit three controlled lighting studies, one exposure/tonal comparison, two attributed references, a value analysis, one before/after revision and an ethical-editing disclosure.
weeks.rubric: Lighting observations and vocabulary 20 · controlled studies 25 · tonal structure and technical application 25 · critique and revision 15 · research, editing disclosure and reflection 15.

weeks.title: Sequence, Documentary Context and Visual Truth
weeks.essential: How can sequence, captions and context influence the meaning of documentary images, and what limits should an artist disclose?

vocab.Sequence: An intentional order that changes how images are read together.
vocab.Caption: Text that identifies or contextualizes an image without claiming more than the evidence supports.
vocab.Staging: Arranging or directing elements before an image is made.
vocab.Corroboration: Independent evidence that helps verify a claim or context.

weeks.worked: Create six drawings or photographs of a simple everyday process. Make one neutral sequence and one reordered sequence. Compare how the inferred story changes even though the individual frames are identical.
stages: Observe a six-step everyday process and list what can be directly seen versus what requires explanation.
Research one attributed documentary image sequence and record creator, source and documented context.
Create a six-frame sequence with accurate captions, then deliberately reorder the same frames and record how interpretation changes.
Ask a reviewer what story they infer from each order. Revise captions or sequence where interpretation depends on unsupported assumptions.
Explain observation versus interpretation versus claim; disclose staging, editing and missing context.
weeks.assignment: Submit one six-frame original sequence, one reordered comparison, accurate captions, one attributed documentary reference, reviewer response and a final limitations statement.
weeks.rubric: Sequence analysis and vocabulary 20 · six-frame study 25 · captions/context accuracy 25 · critique and revision 15 · research, ethics and limitations 15.

weeks.title: Letterform, Readability and Visual Hierarchy
weeks.essential: How do letterform, spacing, scale and contrast make information readable and establish hierarchy?

vocab.Legibility: How easily individual characters can be distinguished.
vocab.Readability: How comfortably text can be read across words, lines and blocks.
vocab.Hierarchy: The visual order that signals what should be noticed first, second and later.
vocab.Tracking: The overall spacing across a range of letters.

weeks.worked: Set the same title, subtitle and paragraph three ways: equal size, exaggerated hierarchy and balanced hierarchy. Compare what a reader notices first and whether any version becomes difficult to read.
stages: Observe three layouts and map title, subtitle, body and supporting text by size, spacing and contrast.
Research two attributed examples of typographic design from an archive, public-information system or established design collection.
Create six letterform/spacing tests and three hierarchy thumbnails using one or two type families or hand-lettered styles.
Run a legibility test at normal and reduced size. Revise one layout based on where readers hesitate or misread.
Archive the final hierarchy, explain spacing and contrast choices and identify one accessibility limitation.
weeks.assignment: Submit six typography tests, three hierarchy thumbnails, one developed composition, two attributed references, legibility-test notes and one documented revision.
weeks.rubric: Vocabulary and visual analysis 20 · letterform/spacing studies 20 · hierarchy and developed layout 30 · legibility test/revision 15 · research and presentation 15.

weeks.title: Layout, Grids and Visual Systems
weeks.essential: How can grids, alignment, spacing and repetition organize information without making every design look the same?

vocab.Grid: An underlying system of columns, rows or modules used to organize placement.
vocab.Alignment: A visible relationship created when edges, centers or baselines line up.
vocab.Module: A repeatable spatial unit within a layout system.
vocab.White space: Unoccupied space used intentionally to separate, group or emphasize information.

weeks.worked: Create the same one-page event notice on a one-column grid, a two-column grid and a modular grid. Compare navigation, balance and unused space before choosing one to refine.
stages: Mark alignment lines and grouping patterns on three existing layouts without judging style.
Research two attributed graphic-design examples and identify how each uses grid, spacing and repetition.
Build three grid systems with identical content so layout remains the tested variable.
Ask a reviewer to locate title, date, action and source quickly. Revise where navigation fails.
Explain which grid was chosen, which constraints helped and where deliberate exceptions improve communication.
weeks.assignment: Submit three grid studies, one developed informational composition, two attributed references, a timed navigation test, one before/after revision and a system explanation.
weeks.rubric: Grid/alignment vocabulary 20 · controlled layout studies 25 · developed composition 25 · navigation test/revision 15 · research/explanation 15.

weeks.title: Information Design and Ethical Claims
weeks.essential: How can visual design clarify evidence without exaggerating, hiding uncertainty or misleading the viewer?

vocab.Scale: The proportional size used to represent or compare information.
vocab.Source note: A traceable citation identifying where information came from.
vocab.Uncertainty: A stated limit in what data or evidence can support.
vocab.Visual emphasis: A design choice that increases attention to selected information.

weeks.worked: Use a tiny fictional data set. Design one honest chart and one deliberately misleading chart using distorted scale, then redesign the misleading version and annotate exactly what made it deceptive.
stages: Observe three information graphics and identify title, source, scale, labels, emphasis and missing context.
Research one reputable public-information graphic and trace its source/data note.
Create an evidence-grounded infographic from a small teacher-approved or fictional data set. Label scale, source and uncertainty.
Ask a viewer what claim they think the graphic supports. Revise any feature that causes overclaiming.
Write the strongest supported claim, one unsupported claim and one design decision that protects against misinterpretation.
weeks.assignment: Submit one source/data record, two layout drafts, one final infographic, a misleading-scale comparison, reviewer notes, revision evidence and a limitations statement.
weeks.rubric: Evidence/claim vocabulary 20 · source/scale accuracy 25 · final design 25 · comprehension review/revision 15 · ethical reasoning/limitations 15.

weeks.title: Art in Cultural Context
weeks.essential: How can artists study work from different cultures and periods with attribution, context and respect rather than reducing it to stereotypes?

vocab.Context: Historical, cultural, social and material circumstances shaping how work is made and understood.
vocab.Attribution: Identifying maker, culture, community, collection or source as accurately as evidence permits.
vocab.Interpretation: A reasoned explanation supported by visible and contextual evidence.
vocab.Stereotype: An oversimplified generalization applied to a group or culture.

weeks.worked: Compare two attributed artworks sharing a broad function such as commemoration or storytelling but coming from different documented contexts. List visible similarities first, contextual differences second, and avoid claiming either work represents an entire culture.
stages: Describe two artworks using only visible evidence before reading context.
Research creator/culture, date or period, material, setting/function and collection/source for each work.
Create a comparative visual study inspired by a shared formal problem—not by copying sacred, restricted or culturally specific imagery.
Review your comparison for unsupported generalizations, missing attribution and language that treats a culture as monolithic.
Revise the analysis and explain how context changed your interpretation.
weeks.assignment: Submit two attributed artwork records, a visible-evidence comparison, contextual research, an original formal-response study, stereotype-check notes, revision and reflection.
weeks.rubric: Description/context vocabulary 20 · attribution/research 25 · comparative analysis 20 · original response/revision 20 · respectful communication/limitations 15.

weeks.title: Community Brief and Collaborative Design
weeks.essential: How can an artist translate a community need or audience goal into a respectful creative brief and revisable proposal?

vocab.Brief: A concise document defining audience, purpose, constraints, deliverables and success criteria.
vocab.Stakeholder: A person or group affected by or involved in a project.
vocab.Constraint: A real limit involving time, place, materials, access, safety, budget or requirements.
vocab.Iteration: A revised version created after testing or feedback.

weeks.worked: Draft a fictional library poster brief: audience, purpose, required information, size, accessibility needs, deadline and no-purchase material limit. Create two thumbnails and revise one after criterion-based feedback.
stages: Observe a public/community communication need and identify audience, purpose, location and constraints without collecting private information.
Research two examples of community-facing design or public art and record creator/organization, purpose and source.
Write a one-page creative brief, then produce at least three concept thumbnails meeting the same brief.
Ask an appropriate reviewer to respond to the stated criteria, not taste. Record accepted and rejected feedback with reasons.
Revise one proposal and show brief → concepts → feedback → final direction.
weeks.assignment: Submit a one-page brief, stakeholder/constraint map, three thumbnails, one developed proposal, feedback record, revision comparison and privacy/accessibility note.
weeks.rubric: Brief/problem definition 20 · constraints/stakeholder reasoning 20 · concept development 25 · feedback/revision 20 · presentation/accessibility/privacy 15.

weeks.title: Curating a Foundations Exhibition
weeks.essential: How can selection, sequence, labels, access and spatial planning help an exhibition communicate a coherent idea?

vocab.Curation: Selecting, organizing and contextualizing works for a stated purpose.
vocab.Wall text: Brief interpretive or informational text supporting an exhibition.
vocab.Sequence: The order in which viewers encounter works or ideas.
vocab.Access consideration: A choice that helps more people perceive, navigate or understand an exhibition.

weeks.worked: Choose five prior practice works with different strengths. Make two exhibition sequences—chronological and thematic. Write a short wall text for each and compare which order better supports the curatorial question.
stages: Review accumulated work and identify recurring questions, techniques and changes rather than simply choosing favorites.
Research one museum, school or community exhibition and record how labels, sequence and access are handled.
Select 6–10 works or studies and create two floor-plan or screen-order options with accurate labels.
Ask a reviewer to move through the exhibition without coaching. Record where sequence or labels create confusion.
Revise selection, order, labels or access notes and write a curatorial statement naming strengths and limits.
weeks.assignment: Submit a 6–10 work checklist, two sequence plans, final floor plan/screen order, labels, wall text, access considerations, reviewer notes and revision evidence.
weeks.rubric: Curatorial vocabulary/question 20 · selection/sequencing 25 · labels/wall text/floor plan 25 · viewer test/revision 15 · access/reflection 15.

weeks.title: Independent Capstone Studio
weeks.essential: How can an artist independently define, research, prototype, revise and complete an original work that synthesizes prior learning?

vocab.Synthesis: Combining multiple learned methods or ideas into a purposeful new whole.
vocab.Prototype: An early version used to test structure, material, composition or feasibility.
vocab.Scope: What a project will and will not attempt within available time and resources.
vocab.Decision log: A concise record of major choices, evidence and revisions.

weeks.worked: Write a capstone proposal around one question. Choose three prior techniques to combine. Make three small prototypes testing different uncertainties. Select one direction using explicit criteria, then define a scope limit that keeps the project achievable.
stages: Review Weeks 1–34 and identify three techniques, questions or methods worth synthesizing.
Research at least two attributed artists/works and one technical source relevant to the chosen problem.
Write a proposal, define scope and create three prototypes, each testing a different uncertainty.
Select and develop one direction. Conduct a critique against proposal criteria and preserve at least one meaningful revision.
Complete the work to a defensible stopping point, document it accurately, and write a decision log with limitations and next steps.
weeks.assignment: Submit capstone proposal, source record, three prototypes, selection criteria, developed work documentation, critique notes, before/after revision, decision log and limitations.
weeks.rubric: Proposal/scope/research 20 · prototype investigation 20 · technical application 20 · original decisions/revision 20 · documentation/defense readiness 20.

weeks.title: Portfolio Exhibition and Artist Defense
weeks.essential: How can a learner use direct evidence to defend artistic growth, technical decisions, revision and portfolio selection across a full year?

vocab.Artist defense: A structured explanation of decisions supported by artifacts and evidence.
vocab.Portfolio coherence: A purposeful relationship among selected works rather than simple quantity.
vocab.Limitation: A clear statement of what the evidence or project does not establish.

weeks.worked: Choose one early study and one later work addressing a related problem. Make one claim about growth, point to a visible artifact in each, compare the difference, and state a limited conclusion. Repeat for technique, revision and independent decision-making.
stages: Review the full-year archive and select evidence representing observation, technique, experimentation, revision, context/research and independent work.
Prepare accurate labels, sources, dates and process notes. Identify at least one early/later comparison and one unsuccessful experiment that taught something useful.
Curate 8–12 representative items or studies and prepare a concise artist statement plus evidence map.
Present the portfolio to an educator/reviewer using evidence chains. Answer questions about choices, revision, limitations, sources and next goals.
Revise portfolio or defense notes after review. Archive the final packet and identify one Grade 10 readiness target.
weeks.assignment: Submit an 8–12 item curated portfolio or documented equivalent, artist statement, evidence map, early/later comparison, attribution record, oral/written defense, reviewer notes, one revision and a Grade 10 readiness target.
weeks.rubric: Portfolio selection/coherence 20 · technical/creative evidence 20 · growth/revision evidence 20 · Artist Defense/reasoning 20 · attribution/presentation/next-step reflection 20.
